items.title: Constitutional Bodies — Overview & Distinction
items.body:
### Constitutional vs statutory vs executive bodies

**In one line**
A 'constitutional body' is one that the Constitution itself creates by name, which is what gives it independence from the government of the day.

**Why it is asked**
Almost every year the exam gives a list and asks 'which of these is NOT a constitutional body'. Knowing the source of each body is the whole game.

**The story**
India's watchdog institutions do not all come from the same place. Some are written into the Constitution, some are made by an ordinary law of Parliament, and some are set up by a simple decision of the Cabinet. The deeper the source, the harder it is for a government to weaken the body — a change written into the Constitution needs a special-majority amendment, while a Cabinet body can be reshaped overnight. That is why the **source test** matters so much.

**Picture it**

| Type | How it is created | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Constitutional | Named or created by the Constitution | ECI (324), UPSC/SPSC (315-323), CAG (148), Finance Commission (280), NCSC (338), NCST (338A), NCBC (338B), Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (350B), GST Council (279A), Attorney General (76), Advocate General (165) |
| Statutory | Created by an Act of Parliament | NHRC, Central Information Commission, Lokpal, Central Vigilance Commission, National Commission for Women |
| Executive | Created by a Cabinet resolution | NITI Aayog (2015) |

**Terms explained**
- **Statutory body** — one set up by a statute, that is, an ordinary law passed by Parliament.
- **Executive body** — one set up by a decision of the Council of Ministers, with no law or constitutional article behind it.
- **Autonomy** — the freedom to work without taking orders from the executive.

**Don't confuse**
- **NITI Aayog** (2015, executive) replaced the Planning Commission but is **not** a constitutional or statutory body.
- **NHRC, CVC and Lokpal** are **statutory**, not constitutional.
- The **Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities** (Art 350B) **is** constitutional, even though it sounds minor.

**Remember it**
Constitutional = written into the **Constitution**; Statutory = written into a **statute**; Executive = just a **Cabinet note**.

**TL;DR**
- Constitutional bodies get their power directly from the Constitution and are hard to weaken.
- Statutory bodies come from an Act (NHRC, CVC, Lokpal); executive bodies from a Cabinet resolution (NITI Aayog).
- Learn the article for each constitutional body: ECI 324, UPSC 315-323, CAG 148, Finance Commission 280.
- The common trap is treating NITI Aayog or NHRC as constitutional — they are not.
keyPoints: Constitutional bodies derive authority directly from the Constitution; they are autonomous and independent.
NITI Aayog (executive, 2015) and NHRC/CIC/Lokpal (statutory) are NOT constitutional bodies.
Key articles: ECI 324, UPSC/SPSC 315-323, CAG 148, Finance Commission 280, Inter-State Council 263.
Social-justice commissions: NCSC 338, NCST 338A, NCBC 338B; Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities 350B.
GST Council is under Article 279A; Attorney General 76 and Advocate General 165 are law officers.
items.mnemonic: Constitutional = written into the Constitution; Statutory = written into a statute; Executive = a Cabinet note.

items.title: Election Commission of India (Article 324)
items.body:
### The Election Commission of India

**In one line**
The Election Commission of India (ECI) is the independent referee that runs national and state elections, created by **Article 324**.

**Why it is asked**
The exam tests its exact scope (which elections it runs), when it became a three-member body, and the removal rules — all common statement-based traps.

**The story**
Free elections need an umpire the government cannot bully. So Article 324 hands the ECI the 'superintendence, direction and control' of elections to **Parliament, the State Legislatures, and the offices of the President and Vice-President**. Note what is **missing** — it does **not** run local-body (panchayat and municipal) elections; those belong to the State Election Commission.

Its shape changed over time. Set up in **1950**, it was a **single-member** body for nearly four decades. Two Election Commissioners were added in **1989**, abolished in January **1990**, and from **October 1993** it has been a permanent **three-member** body (the Chief Election Commissioner plus two Election Commissioners). All three have equal powers and settle disagreements by majority vote.

Independence is protected by the removal rule. The **CEC** can be removed only in the **same way as a Supreme Court judge** (a hard impeachment process); but an ordinary **Election Commissioner** can be removed **only on the CEC's recommendation**. This asymmetry shields the CEC strongly and the ECs a little less.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Rule |
|---|---|
| Elections run | Parliament, State Legislatures, President, Vice-President |
| Members (since Oct 1993) | CEC + 2 ECs = 3 |
| Term | 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier |
| CEC removal | Like a Supreme Court judge |
| EC removal | Only on the CEC's recommendation |

**Terms explained**
- **Superintendence** — overall supervision and control.
- **Model Code of Conduct** — a set of do's and don'ts for parties and candidates once elections are announced; the ECI frames and enforces it.
- **Delimitation** — fixing the boundaries of constituencies.

**Don't confuse**
- ECI runs **Assembly and Parliament** polls; the **State Election Commission** runs **local-body** polls — a very common trap.
- The number of members is **not fixed** by the Constitution; it is currently three by practice/law.
- Deciding how tax money is shared is the **Finance Commission's** job, never the ECI's.

**Remember it**
'**324 = the election umpire for the big polls**, not for village and town polls.'

**TL;DR**
- Article 324 gives the ECI control of Parliament, State Legislature, President and Vice-President elections.
- It has been a permanent three-member body since October 1993.
- Term is 6 years or age 65; the CEC is removed like a Supreme Court judge.
- It does not run local-body elections (that is the State Election Commission's role).
keyPoints: Article 324 covers Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President — NOT local bodies.
ECI was single-member until 1989 and permanently multi-member (3 members) from October 1993.
CEC removed like a Supreme Court judge; an EC/Regional Commissioner only on the CEC's recommendation.
Term of CEC/ECs: 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier; salary equal to a Supreme Court judge.
ECI registers parties, allots symbols, and enforces the Model Code of Conduct; State-level help from the Chief Electoral Officer.

items.title: UPSC & SPSC (Articles 315-323)
items.body:
### The Public Service Commissions

**In one line**
The UPSC is the Union's independent recruiting agency for the higher civil services, and each state has its own version, the SPSC — both set up by **Articles 315-323**.

**Why it is asked**
The favourite trap is the contrast between the UPSC and the SPSC — who appoints, who removes, and the age limit — plus the fact that UPSC advice is not binding.

**The story**
To keep recruitment free of political favouritism, the Constitution created a permanent, independent commission. The **UPSC** usually has **9 to 11 members** appointed by the **President**; the only condition the Constitution imposes is that about **half** of them must have held office for **at least ten years** under the Union or a State. A member serves **6 years or until age 65**.

Independence is guarded three ways: expenses are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India** (so the legislature cannot squeeze its budget), service conditions cannot be worsened after appointment, and the **chairman is barred from any further government job** afterwards. Removal for **misbehaviour** needs a **Supreme Court inquiry whose advice binds the President**.

But its power is limited: its recommendations are **advisory only**, and if the government fails to consult it, the aggrieved employee has **no remedy in court**. The President may even exclude some posts from its scope, though such rules must lie before Parliament for **14 days**.

The **State Public Service Commission** mirrors the UPSC with three key differences, which the exam loves.

**Picture it**

| Feature | UPSC | SPSC |
|---|---|---|
| Appointed by | President | Governor |
| Age limit | 65 | 62 |
| Removed by | President | President only (not the Governor) |

**Terms explained**
- **Advisory** — the government should consult it, but is not legally bound to accept its advice.
- **Charged on the Consolidated Fund** — paid automatically, not subject to the legislature's annual vote.
- **Joint SPSC (JSPSC)** — a single commission for two or more states; this one is **statutory**, not constitutional.

**Don't confuse**
- The SPSC member is **appointed by the Governor** but can be **removed only by the President** — the single most-tested point.
- UPSC age limit is **65**, SPSC is **62**.
- A **Joint** SPSC is statutory; a normal UPSC/SPSC is constitutional.

**Remember it**
'The **Governor gives** the SPSC job (age 62), but only the **President can take it away**.'

**TL;DR**
- UPSC (Articles 315-323): 9-11 members, appointed by the President, term 6 years or age 65.
- Its advice is not binding, and failure to consult gives no court remedy.
- SPSC: appointed by the Governor, age limit 62, but removed only by the President.
- A Joint State Public Service Commission is a statutory, not a constitutional, body.
keyPoints: UPSC: Articles 315-323; usually 9-11 members appointed by the President; term 6 years or age 65.
About half the members must have held office 10 years under the Union or a State — the only constitutional condition.
UPSC recommendations are advisory; failure to consult gives no judicial remedy; expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
SPSC members are appointed by the Governor (age limit 62) but can be removed only by the President.
A Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC) is a statutory, not a constitutional, body.
items.mnemonic: Governor gives the SPSC job (62), but only the President can take it away.

items.title: CAG (Art 148) & Finance Commission (Art 280)
items.body:
### CAG and the Finance Commission

**In one line**
The CAG is the auditor who checks how the government spent public money, and the Finance Commission advises how tax money is shared between the Centre and the States.

**Why it is asked**
Two classic traps: that India's CAG only audits (unlike Britain's), and that the Finance Commission's advice is **not binding**.

**The story**
The **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)**, under **Article 148**, is the 'guardian of the public purse'. The President appoints the CAG, who serves **6 years or until age 65** and can be removed **only like a Supreme Court judge**; afterwards the CAG holds **no further office**, so there is no reward to tempt leniency. The CAG audits the accounts of the Union, the States and the Union Territories with a legislature, and files **three reports** (Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts, and Public Undertakings) that the **Public Accounts Committee** then examines.

Here is the key contrast. India's CAG is **only an Auditor General** — it checks spending **after** it happens and has **no control over the issue of money** from the treasury. Britain's officer is **both Comptroller and Auditor General**, so in Britain money can be drawn only **with** his approval. India chose post-facto audit, not pre-audit.

The **Finance Commission**, under **Article 280**, is set up by the President **every fifth year**. It has a **chairman and four members**, all of whom can be reappointed. It recommends how central taxes are divided with the States, the grants-in-aid they receive, and steps to boost State funds for panchayats and municipalities — but, like the UPSC, its recommendations are **advisory only**. The **16th Finance Commission** is chaired by **Arvind Panagariya**, with an award period running from **2026-27**.

**Picture it**

| Body | Article | Term | Advice binding? |
|---|---|---|---|
| CAG | 148 | 6 years / age 65 | Not applicable (it audits) |
| Finance Commission | 280 | Every 5th year | No — advisory only |

**Terms explained**
- **Comptroller** — an officer who controls the release of money before it is spent (India's CAG is NOT one).
- **Grants-in-aid** — money the Centre gives States to meet needs their own revenue cannot.
- **Devolution** — the share of central taxes passed down to the States.

**Don't confuse**
- India's CAG audits **after** spending; it is **not** a Comptroller like Britain's.
- The Finance Commission (Art 280) is **not** the GST Council (Art 279A), and its advice is not binding.
- The CAG submits **three** reports, examined by the **PAC**, not by itself.

**Remember it**
'India's CAG **counts the money after it is spent**; Britain's also **guards the gate before it is spent**.'

**TL;DR**
- CAG (Article 148): term 6 years or age 65; removed only like a Supreme Court judge; ineligible for further office.
- India's CAG only audits post-facto, with no control over the issue of money.
- Finance Commission (Article 280): set up every fifth year, chairman plus four members, advice is advisory.
- The 16th Finance Commission is chaired by Arvind Panagariya (award period from 2026-27).
keyPoints: CAG (Article 148): term 6 years/age 65; removed only like a Supreme Court judge; ineligible for further office.
CAG audits after expenditure and has no control over the issue of money — unlike Britain's CAG (both Comptroller and Auditor).
CAG submits three reports (Appropriation, Finance, Public Undertakings); acts as guide to the Public Accounts Committee.
Finance Commission (Article 280): constituted every fifth year; chairman + 4 members; recommendations advisory.
The 16th Finance Commission is chaired by Arvind Panagariya, covering the award period from 2026-27.

items.title: Social-Justice Commissions & Law Officers
items.body:
### Social-justice commissions and the law officers

**In one line**
A set of commissions protects SCs, STs and backward classes, while the Attorney General and Advocate General are the government's top lawyers.

**Why it is asked**
The exam tests which amendment created each commission and the article number, plus the appoint/qualify contrast between the Attorney General and the Advocate General.

**The story**
At first **Article 338** gave only a single **Special Officer for SCs and STs**. The **89th Amendment, 2003** split this into two full commissions: the **NCSC (Article 338)** and the **NCST (Article 338A)**. Each has a chairperson, a vice-chairperson and three members appointed by the President, and each carries the **powers of a civil court** — it can summon people and demand documents. The **NCBC** (for backward classes) was only a statutory body under a 1993 Act until the **102nd Amendment, 2018** made it constitutional through **Article 338B**; the same amendment added **Article 342A**, letting the President specify socially and educationally backward classes. These bodies trace back to **Article 340**, under which commissions like Kaka Kalelkar (1953) and Mandal (1979) were appointed, and the **Indra Sawhney case (1992)** which pushed for a permanent body.

The **law officers** advise the government in court. The **Attorney General** (Article 76) is the Union's highest law officer; the **Advocate General** (Article 165) is the state's equivalent. Both may speak in their legislature but cannot vote.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Attorney General (Art 76) | Advocate General (Art 165) |
|---|---|---|
| Appointed by | President | Governor |
| Qualification | Qualified to be a Supreme Court judge | Qualified to be a High Court judge |
| Tenure | Pleasure of the President | Pleasure of the Governor |
| Privilege | Speak in Parliament, no vote | Speak in the State legislature, no vote |

Finally, the **Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities** (Article 350B) was added by the **7th Amendment, 1956** on the advice of the **States Reorganisation Commission**, and reports to the President on safeguards for linguistic minorities.

**Terms explained**
- **SEBC** — socially and educationally backward classes, the groups the NCBC and Article 342A deal with.
- **Powers of a civil court** — the authority to summon witnesses, demand documents and record evidence on oath.
- **At the pleasure of** — holds office for as long as the appointing authority wishes, with no fixed term.

**Don't confuse**
- **89th Amendment (2003)** created NCSC and NCST; **102nd Amendment (2018)** gave the NCBC constitutional status — easy to swap.
- The **Attorney General** is qualified like a **Supreme Court** judge; the **Advocate General** like a **High Court** judge.
- The **Solicitor General** is **not** mentioned in Article 76 (a statutory office).

**Remember it**
'**338, 338A, 338B = SC, ST, Backward Classes** — three doors on the same corridor.'

**TL;DR**
- 89th Amendment (2003) split the SC/ST body into NCSC (Art 338) and NCST (Art 338A), each with civil-court powers.
- NCBC became constitutional via the 102nd Amendment, 2018 (Article 338B); Article 342A lets the President specify backward classes.
- Attorney General (Art 76): appointed by the President, qualified as an SC judge; Advocate General (Art 165): appointed by the Governor, qualified as an HC judge.
- Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Art 350B) was added by the 7th Amendment, 1956.
keyPoints: 89th Amendment (2003) split the SC/ST body into NCSC (Art 338) and NCST (Art 338A); each has civil-court powers.
NCBC gained constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment, 2018 (Article 338B); Article 342A lets the President specify SEBCs.
Attorney General (Art 76): appointed by President, qualified as SC judge, holds office at President's pleasure.
Advocate General (Art 165): appointed by Governor, qualified as HC judge — the State's highest law officer.
Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Art 350B) added by the 7th Amendment, 1956 on the States Reorganisation Commission's advice.

items.title: GST Council & Current Office-Holders (Sep 2026)
items.body:
### The GST Council and who holds office now

**In one line**
The GST Council is the joint Centre-State body that decides GST rates and rules, and this note also lists who currently heads each constitutional authority.

**Why it is asked**
The voting formula (Centre one-third, States two-thirds, three-fourths to pass) is a favourite, and current office-holders are standard current-affairs questions.

**The story**
When the Goods and Services Tax replaced a tangle of indirect taxes, India needed one forum where the Centre and all the States could set rates together. The **101st Amendment** created the **GST Council** under **Article 279A** (GST rolled out on 1 July 2017). The **Union Finance Minister chairs it ex-officio**, and every State sends its Finance or Taxation Minister. To stop either side dominating, the votes are weighted: the **Centre gets one-third** and **all the States together get two-thirds**, and a decision needs a **three-fourths weighted majority** of those present and voting. Neither the Centre nor the States can push a change through alone — a textbook example of cooperative federalism.

**Picture it — current office-holders (verified September 2026)**

| Office | Article | Holder |
|---|---|---|
| Chief Election Commissioner (26th) | 324 | Gyanesh Kumar (since 19 Feb 2025) |
| Comptroller and Auditor General (15th) | 148 | K. Sanjay Murthy (since 21 Nov 2024) |
| Attorney General of India (16th) | 76 | R. Venkataramani (since 1 Oct 2022) |
| Chairman, UPSC | 316 | Ajay Kumar (IAS) |
| Chairman, 16th Finance Commission | 280 | Arvind Panagariya |
| Chair, GST Council (ex-officio) | 279A | Nirmala Sitharaman (Union FM) |
| Chairman, NCSC | 338 | Kishor Makwana |
| Chairman, NCST | 338A | Antar Singh Arya |
| Chairperson, NCBC | 338B | Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti (since 18 Mar 2026) |

**Terms explained**
- **Ex-officio** — holds the post automatically by virtue of another office (here, because she is the Union Finance Minister).
- **Weighted vote** — a vote that counts for more or less depending on who casts it, rather than one-person-one-vote.
- **Cooperative federalism** — the Centre and States working jointly through shared institutions.

**Don't confuse**
- The GST Council (Art 279A) is **not** the Finance Commission (Art 280).
- A decision needs **three-fourths** of the weighted votes, not a simple majority.
- The NCBC chair changed in 2026 to **Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti** — keep office-holders current.

**Remember it**
'GST Council: **Centre one-third, States two-thirds, three-fourths to pass**.'

**TL;DR**
- GST Council (Article 279A) was created by the 101st Amendment and is chaired ex-officio by the Union Finance Minister.
- Voting: Centre one-third, States two-thirds; decisions need a three-fourths weighted majority.
- As of Sep 2026: CEC Gyanesh Kumar, CAG K. Sanjay Murthy, Attorney General R. Venkataramani, UPSC chair Ajay Kumar.
- 16th Finance Commission chair Arvind Panagariya; GST Council chair Nirmala Sitharaman; NCBC chair Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti.
keyPoints: GST Council (Article 279A) created by the 101st Amendment; chaired ex-officio by the Union Finance Minister.
GST Council voting: Centre one-third, States two-thirds; decisions need a three-fourths weighted majority.
As of Sep 2026: CEC Gyanesh Kumar; CAG K. Sanjay Murthy; Attorney General R. Venkataramani; UPSC Chairman Ajay Kumar.
16th Finance Commission Chairman Arvind Panagariya; GST Council chair Nirmala Sitharaman (Union FM).
NCSC Chairman Kishor Makwana, NCST Chairman Antar Singh Arya, NCBC Chairperson Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti (since 18 Mar 2026); APPSC HQ Vijayawada (Chairman + 9 members).

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Constitutional & Statutory Authorities (2026)
items.body:
### Andhra Pradesh's authorities

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh has its own public service commission and local-government bodies drawn from the Constitution, plus statutory watchdogs created by state law.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC is the recruiting body for this very exam, and the AP-specific bodies (SEC, State Finance Commission, Lokayukta) are high-probability state-GK items.

**The story**
The **Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission (APPSC)** is a State Public Service Commission under **Articles 315-323**. As with every SPSC, the **Governor appoints** its Chairman and members, but they can be **removed only by the President** (Article 317) — the safeguard that keeps it independent. Its headquarters is at **Vijayawada**, and the present Chairman, as of September 2026, is **Prof. C. Sashidhar** holding Full Additional Charge.

Two constitutional bodies serve local government. The **State Election Commission** (Articles 243K and 243ZA) runs panchayat and municipal elections — not Assembly elections, which stay with the ECI. The **State Finance Commission** (Articles 243-I and 243-Y) is set up by the Governor every five years to recommend how funds reach local bodies.

Alongside these sit **statutory** watchdogs created by ordinary law, not the Constitution: the **Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta** (AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983), the **AP State Human Rights Commission** (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993) and the **AP State Commission for Women**.

**Picture it**

| Body | Provision | Set up by | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| State Election Commission | Art 243K / 243ZA | Governor | Panchayat and municipal elections |
| State Finance Commission | Art 243-I / 243-Y | Governor, every 5 years | Funds and grants to local bodies |
| Lokayukta | AP Act, 1983 | State statute | Anti-corruption ombudsman |

**Terms explained**
- **Ombudsman** — an official who investigates complaints of corruption or maladministration against public servants.
- **Full Additional Charge** — temporarily heading a post in addition to one's own, until a regular appointment is made.
- **Local body** — a panchayat (rural) or municipality (urban) elected government.

**Don't confuse**
- The **State Election Commission** runs **local-body** polls; the **ECI** runs **Assembly and Parliament** polls.
- APPSC members are **appointed by the Governor** but **removed only by the President**.
- The **Lokayukta** and the **Human Rights Commission** are **statutory**, not constitutional.

**Remember it**
'In AP, the **Governor appoints** the watchdogs, but only the **President removes** the APPSC.'

**TL;DR**
- APPSC (Arts 315-323): Governor appoints, President removes (Art 317); HQ Vijayawada; Chairman Prof. C. Sashidhar (FAC, Sep 2026).
- State Election Commission (243K/243ZA) runs local-body polls; the ECI runs Assembly and Parliament polls.
- State Finance Commission (243-I/243-Y) is set up by the Governor every five years.
- AP Lokayukta (1983 Act), AP State Human Rights Commission (1993 Act) and the Women's Commission are statutory bodies.
keyPoints: APPSC under Arts 315-323; Governor appoints, President removes (Art 317); HQ Vijayawada; Chairman Prof. C. Sashidhar (FAC, Sep 2026)
AP State Election Commission (Art 243K/243ZA) runs local-body polls; ECI runs Assembly/Parliament polls
AP State Finance Commission constituted by Governor every 5 years (Arts 243-I & 243-Y)
AP Lokayukta & Upa-Lokayukta = statutory ombudsman under the AP Lokayukta Act, 1983
AP SHRC (Protection of Human Rights Act 1993) and AP Women's Commission are statutory, not constitutional, bodies
items.source: Constitution (Arts 243, 315-323) / official AP bodies; APPSC chair verified via Wikipedia as of Sep 2026

items.title: PYQ Precision — PAC, NDC & Presidential Election
items.body:
### Three high-frequency PYQ facts

**In one line**
Three exam-tested details that trip students up: the make-up of the Public Accounts Committee, who sits on the National Development Council, and how the President's votes are counted.

**Why it is asked**
Each has appeared as a UPSC prelims statement question, and the wrong options are built from very small factual slips.

**The story**
The **Public Accounts Committee (PAC)** is Parliament's spending watchdog. It has **22 members — 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha** — serves a **one-year** term, and (by convention since 1967) is **chaired by an Opposition member**. A minister cannot be a member. It studies the **CAG's** audit reports, which is why the CAG is called its 'friend, philosopher and guide'.

The **National Development Council (NDC)** is an **extra-constitutional, non-statutory** body set up by a Cabinet resolution in 1952 — it is **not** in the Constitution at all. Its members are the **Prime Minister (head), all Union Cabinet Ministers, the Chief Ministers of all States, the administrators of Union Territories, and NITI Aayog members**. The common trap: the **Finance Commission Chairman is NOT** a member.

For the **President's election**, each **MLA's vote value = (the State's 1971 population ÷ the number of elected MLAs) ÷ 1000**, so it **differs from State to State**. Every **MP**, whether from the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha, has the **same** vote value, and the total value of all MPs' votes is kept roughly equal to that of all MLAs — the Union-State parity built into the system.

**Picture it**

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| PAC strength | 22 (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha) |
| PAC chair | Opposition, by convention |
| NDC and Finance Commission chair | Not a member |
| MP vote value | Equal for all MPs |

**Terms explained**
- **Extra-constitutional** — not created by, or mentioned in, the Constitution.
- **Proportional representation by single transferable vote** — the counting method used to elect the President.
- **Union-State parity** — balancing the combined vote weight of MPs against that of all MLAs.

**Don't confuse**
- PAC chair is from the **Opposition**, not the ruling party.
- The **Finance Commission Chairman** is **not** an NDC member.
- An **MLA's** vote value varies by State; an **MP's** value is the same everywhere.

**Remember it**
'PAC = **22 (15 + 7)**; NDC = **everyone but the Finance Commission chair**; MP votes **all equal**.'

**TL;DR**
- PAC: 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha), one-year term, chaired by the Opposition, examines CAG reports.
- NDC: extra-constitutional (1952); members are the PM, Union Cabinet, all CMs, UT administrators and NITI Aayog, but not the Finance Commission chair.
- President's election: each MLA's vote value varies by State; every MP's value is equal.
- These exact numbers and the excluded members are where the marks are won or lost.
keyPoints: PAC = 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha); 1-year term; chair from Opposition by convention; examines CAG reports.
A minister cannot be a member of the PAC.
NDC is extra-constitutional/non-statutory (1952); NOT mentioned in the Constitution.
NDC members: PM + all Union Cabinet Ministers + all CMs + UT administrators + NITI Aayog; the Finance Commission Chairman is NOT a member.
President's election: each MLA's vote value varies by State; every MP has equal vote value (Union-State parity).
items.source: UPSC 2013 & 2018 Prelims (Rau's IAS COMPASS); Constitution Arts 54-55, 280

items.title: For Mains — Constitutional Authorities
items.body:
## For Mains — how to use this topic in answers

This topic feeds **Paper III (mains-3)**: clause M3-3 (Constitutional Authorities; local governance) and M3-9 (statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial authorities, role of civil services). Mains answers must argue about the **independence, effectiveness and accountability** of these bodies, not just list their articles.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Rationale | Watchdog bodies check the executive and uphold free elections, honest audit and merit recruitment |
| Safeguards | Removal like a judge, salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, bars on post-retirement office |
| Weaknesses | Executive-driven appointments; advisory-only powers; CAG audits only after the event |
| Reforms | Collegium-style appointments, fixed tenures, performance reporting to Parliament |
| Federal angle | GST Council and the Finance Commission as instruments of cooperative federalism |

**Facts, committees and reports to quote**
- **2nd ARC (Administrative Reforms Commission)** — recommended insulating appointments to watchdog bodies.
- **CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023** — introduced a selection committee (PM, Leader of Opposition, a Union Minister) for Election Commissioners.
- **Anoop Baranwal (2023)** — the Supreme Court pushed for a neutral appointment panel for the ECI.
- **16th Finance Commission** (Arvind Panagariya, award 2026-27 onward) — current fiscal devolution.
- **102nd Amendment, 2018** — constitutional status to the NCBC (Article 338B).

**The AP angle**
As a revenue-dependent successor State after the 2014 bifurcation, Andhra Pradesh leans on **Finance Commission devolution** and uses the **GST Council** to voice State-specific concerns; its **State Election Commission** and **State Finance Commission** show how local governance is funded and run.

**Use in answers**
- Structure: independence (strengths) then effectiveness (gaps) then reforms.
- Quote: Dr B.R. Ambedkar called such bodies the 'bulwarks' of the democratic system.
- Diagram idea: a simple chart of a watchdog body with arrows for appointment (in) and reporting (out) to show where independence is strong and where it is weak.
